options.text: A mixture of hydrocarbons
options.explanation: The crude is many hydrocarbon molecules jumbled together, which is why it must be separated before use.

options.text: A single pure compound
options.explanation: A pure compound would need no separation; the whole point is the mixture of many chains.

options.text: A mixture of elements
options.explanation: The components are compounds of hydrogen and carbon, not free elements.

options.text: A solution of salts in water
options.explanation: Crude oil contains no water or salts; it is hydrocarbons throughout.

questions.stem: Why do molecules of a fraction have similar boiling points?

options.text: Because their hydrocarbon chains have similar lengths
options.explanation: Chain length sets the boiling point, so similar chains condense together as one fraction.

options.text: Because they were distilled at the same temperature
options.explanation: The condensation temperature is a consequence of chain length, not a rule imposed by the apparatus.

options.text: Because they all contain the same number of hydrogen atoms
options.explanation: Hydrogen count varies within a fraction; chain length is the organising feature.

options.text: Because fractions are chemically bonded to each other
options.explanation: Fractions are physical groups of molecules, joined by nothing stronger than mixing.

questions.stem: In the fractionating column, where do vapours with high boiling points condense?

options.text: Near the bottom of the column, where it is hottest
options.explanation: High boiling points need the hot lower region before the vapour turns back to liquid.

options.text: Near the top of the column, where it is coolest
options.explanation: The cool top collects low-boiling vapours; high boilers never make the climb.

options.text: They never condense inside the column at all
options.explanation: Every fraction condenses somewhere on the column; height just depends on boiling point.

options.text: Halfway up, regardless of boiling point
options.explanation: Height tracks boiling point continuously; there is no single fixed floor.

questions.stem: What happens to the crude oil before the vapours enter the column?

options.text: It is heated so that it vaporises
options.explanation: Vaporising first lets the hydrocarbon vapours rise and separate on the gradient.

options.text: It is cooled until it solidifies
options.explanation: Freezing would stop the separation; heat is what mobilises the molecules.

options.text: It is mixed with water to dilute it
options.explanation: No dilution happens; the oil is heated directly before the column.

options.text: It is filtered to remove the alkanes
options.explanation: Alkanes are exactly what is being separated, not removed as debris.

questions.stem: As you move up a fractionating column, what happens to the temperature?

options.text: It decreases, so high-boiling compounds leave lower down
options.explanation: The exam hint of the note: temperature falls with height, sorting fractions by boiling point.

options.text: It increases, pushing heavy molecules upward
options.explanation: The gradient runs the other way: hot at the base, cool at the top.

options.text: It stays constant from bottom to top
options.explanation: A constant temperature would give no separation at all.

options.text: It alternates hot and cold in bands
options.explanation: The column has one smooth gradient, not alternating zones.

questions.stem: Which fraction is used for surfacing roads and roofs?

options.text: Bitumen
options.explanation: The thickest, darkest fraction is the one applied to roads and roofs.

options.text: Fuel oil
options.explanation: Fuel oil powers ships and power stations; it never surfaces roads.

options.text: Diesel
options.explanation: Diesel runs engines; surfacing is bitumen work.

options.text: Kerosene
options.explanation: Kerosene is jet fuel, far too runny for road surfacing.

questions.stem: Why does viscosity increase along the fraction ladder?

options.text: Longer chains attract each other more, so the liquid flows less easily
options.explanation: Greater intermolecular attraction between bigger molecules thickens the liquid.

options.text: Longer chains are lighter, so they sink and thicken
options.explanation: Longer chains are heavier, not lighter, and sinking is not how viscosity works.

options.text: Because fractions are cooled before collection
options.explanation: Cooling is part of the column process, not the cause of the viscosity trend.

options.text: Viscosity does not change along the ladder
options.explanation: The trend is explicit: flow gets harder as chains grow.

questions.stem: A fraction boils between 150 and 240 degrees Celsius. Which fraction is it?

options.text: Kerosene
options.explanation: Kerosene sits at 12-16 carbons and boils across 150-240 degrees in the table.

options.text: Gasoline
options.explanation: Gasoline boils at 40-100 degrees, below the stated window.

options.text: Diesel
options.explanation: Diesel boils at 220-300 degrees, only touching the top of that window.

options.text: Refinery gas
options.explanation: Refinery gas boils below 25 degrees, far under the stated range.

questions.stem: What happens to volatility as molecular size increases?

options.text: Liquids become less volatile because molecules are held more tightly
options.explanation: Stronger attraction between larger molecules makes vaporising harder, lowering volatility.

options.text: Liquids become more volatile as they get thicker
options.explanation: Thicker liquids are the opposite of eager evaporators; the two trends run contrary.

options.text: Volatility stays fixed across the fractions
options.explanation: Volatility falls steadily with size, matching the rising boiling points.

options.text: Volatility depends only on the colour of the fraction
options.explanation: Colour tracks the same ladder but does not cause volatility.

questions.stem: Which pairing of fraction and use is correct?

options.text: Kerosene for jet fuel and refinery gas for domestic heating
options.explanation: The use table pairs kerosene with aircraft and refinery gas with heating and cooking.

options.text: Gasoline for ships and fuel oil for cars
options.explanation: The pairing is reversed: gasoline fuels cars and fuel oil powers ships.

options.text: Diesel for cooking and refinery gas for trucks
options.explanation: Both halves are wrong; diesel engines burn diesel and cooking uses refinery gas.

options.text: Bitumen for jet fuel and kerosene for roads
options.explanation: This swaps the extreme ends of the ladder, where the properties could not differ more.

questions.stem: Which of these is obtained from crude oil?

options.text: Detergents and solvents
options.explanation: The note lists polymers, lubricants, solvents, detergents and adhesives as oil-derived products.

options.text: Natural gas
options.explanation: Natural gas is a separate fossil fuel, not a product distilled from crude oil.

options.text: Iron ore
options.explanation: Iron ore is mined rock with no connection to oil refining.

options.text: Limestone
options.explanation: Limestone is a carbonate rock, unrelated to the fractions of crude oil.

questions.stem: What allows carbon to form such a huge number of organic compounds?

options.text: Its ability to form multiple strong covalent bonds with itself
options.explanation: Carbon chaining to itself builds skeletons of any length, which multiplies the possible compounds.

options.text: Its unusually low boiling point
options.explanation: Carbon itself is not a liquid here; bonding versatility is the point.

options.text: Its radioactive behaviour in fuels
options.explanation: Radioactivity plays no part in organic chemistry bonding.

options.text: Its refusal to react with hydrogen
options.explanation: Hydrocarbons are defined by carbon-hydrogen bonding, so refusal is the opposite of reality.

questions.stem: Which transport uses are based on oil products?

options.text: Cars, trains and aircraft
options.explanation: The note lists modern methods of transport from cars to trains to planes as oil-based.

options.text: Only cars
options.explanation: The reach is far wider than cars; aircraft and trains appear in the same sentence.

options.text: Only electric trains
options.explanation: Electric traction is precisely the case that does not run on oil products here.

options.text: No transport, because oil is too viscous
options.explanation: Refining solves viscosity by sorting fractions to each engine type.

questions.stem: Why is the petrochemical industry described as hugely important?

options.text: Because modern society runs on its fuels and manufactured products
options.explanation: Transport fuels plus polymer and solvent manufacture give the industry its central role.

options.text: Because it supplies drinking water
options.explanation: Water supply is not a petrochemical product in this account.

options.text: Because crude oil is useful exactly as it comes out of the ground
options.explanation: The crude itself is not useful; the separated fractions and their products are.

options.text: Because fractions cannot be modified once separated
options.explanation: Fractions are routinely cracked and modified, which is the next note topic.

questions.stem: Refinery gas is also known by which other name in the exam hint?

options.text: Liquid petroleum gases
options.explanation: The exam hint gives liquid petroleum gases as the alias for refinery gases.

options.text: Paraffin
options.explanation: Paraffin is the alias of kerosene, one rung down the ladder.

options.text: Petrol
options.explanation: Petrol is the everyday name for gasoline, not refinery gas.

options.text: Gas oil
options.explanation: Gas oil is the alias of diesel, further up the ladder than refinery gas.
